To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 57 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p ≥ .115 Trial exclusion rates were not significantly different across conditions ( 2 (2) = 5.87, p = 0.053), and was not significantly associated with any transdiagnostic factor score (all 𝜏 0.081, all p ≥ .115; Supplementary Table 1).
p-values < 0.05 To evaluate model fit, we calculated Bayesian p-values as the proportion of predicted statistics more extreme than the corresponding observed statistic (two-tailed), with p-values < 0.05 indicating circumstances where the model fails to capture the observed data pattern.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Neutral: t (192) = 14.597, p < 0.001, Like vs Dislike: t (192) = 3.982, p < 0.001).
A one-way repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant effect of condition on DT (F (2,384) = 4.18, p = 0.016), with post-hoc Tukey-corrected comparisons showing participants responded significantly faster in the ‘Dislike’ (M =1604 ± 476ms) condition compared to ‘Neutral’ (M = 1698 ± 529ms) (p = 0.009), while other pairwise comparisons were not significant (‘Like’ condition: M = 1667 ± 466ms, Figure 1d).
A learning-rate valence (positive vs negative) by condition (Like, Dislike, Neutral) repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) revealed a significant main effect of learning-rate valence (F (1,192) = 465.51, p < 0.001) and condition (F~(1.27, 243.94)~= 52.27, p < 0.001), and a significant interaction (F~(1.27, 243.82)~= 111.26, p < 0.001), indicating that the relationship between feedback valence and learning varied across conditions (Figure 2a).
Post-hoc pairwise comparisons using Tukey’s adjustment showed the positive learning rate was significantly higher in both the ‘Like’ and ‘Dislike’ conditions than in ‘Neutral’ (both p < 0.001), but did not differ between ‘Like’ and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 1.83, p = 0.162).
For negative learning rates, the ‘Like’ condition showed significantly lower learning rates than both ‘Neutral’ (t (192) = 5.40, p < 0.001) and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 5.26, p < 0.001), which did not significantly differ from each other (t (192) = 1.82, p = 0.166).
For negative learning rates, the ‘Like’ condition showed significantly lower learning rates than both ‘Neutral’ (t (192) = 5.40, p < 0.001) and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 5.26, p < 0.001), which did not significantly differ from each other (t (192) = 1.82, p = 0.166).

Tukey-corrected post-hoc comparisons showed that 𝜏 was significantly higher in both the ‘Like’ (M = 2.14) and ‘Dislike’ (M = 2.20) conditions than in ‘Neutral’ (M = 1.62; Like vs Neutral: t (192) = 25.90, p < 0.001; Dislike vs Neutral: t (192) = 11.93, p < 0.001), indicating more deterministic choice under valenced feedback, but did not differ between ‘Like’ and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 1.10, p = 0.513).
Tukey-corrected post-hoc comparisons showed that 𝜏 was significantly higher in both the ‘Like’ (M = 2.14) and ‘Dislike’ (M = 2.20) conditions than in ‘Neutral’ (M = 1.62; Like vs Neutral: t (192) = 25.90, p < 0.001; Dislike vs Neutral: t (192) = 11.93, p < 0.001), indicating more deterministic choice under valenced feedback, but did not differ between ‘Like’ and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 1.10, p = 0.513).
Tukey-corrected post-hoc comparisons showed that 𝜏 was significantly higher in both the ‘Like’ (M = 2.14) and ‘Dislike’ (M = 2.20) conditions than in ‘Neutral’ (M = 1.62; Like vs Neutral: t (192) = 25.90, p < 0.001; Dislike vs Neutral: t (192) = 11.93, p < 0.001), indicating more deterministic choice under valenced feedback, but did not differ between ‘Like’ and ‘Dislike’ (t (192) = 1.10, p = 0.513).
Indeed, one-sample t-tests confirmed that accuracy exceeded chance (50%) in valenced conditions (Like: t (192) = 28.94, p < 0.001; Dislike: t (192) = 23.02, p < 0.001) but not Neutral (t (192) = 1.24, p = 0.215).

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 139 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 139 data columns across 3 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To fix Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 47 files: 9 data, 24 code, 1 documentation, 12 materials, 1 unknown.
  • We found 8 tabular data files and extracted 139 columns from 3 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex19), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 4 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy.
  • 1 R workspace file (.RData/.rda) contains no reusable tabular data — only fitted models or saved session objects. Such files need R (and the exact packages used) to open and are not machine-readable. Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented .sav/.dta) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: dataList.RData. We ran automated data-quality checks on 139 columns; 41 columns have at least one potential issue (26 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 5 columns with numeric values stored as text; 5 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 4 columns whose values look like personal information; 2 columns with inconsistent category casing; 2 columns whose names become identical when special characters are removed; 2 columns that look like geographic coordinates; 1 column whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 139 columns across 3 data files.

Issues Identified

41 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 22 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 3 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 1 code file.

Calls that install packages in the code

5 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

2 scripts are run by another script with source(), so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

File Run by
brms_config.R brms_regression_models.R, brms_collate.R
main_modelling_run_stan.R run_models_array.R

> save_plot <- function(plot_code, filename, width = 800, height = 600, dpi = 1200) {
>   filepath <- here("output", "plots", "behav", filename)
>   scale <- dpi / 72
>   px_width  <- width * scale
>   px_height <- height * scale
> 
>   # Try default (platform) PNG device first, fallback to Cairo PNG, then PDF
>   tryCatch({
>     png(filepath, width = px_width, height = px_height, res = dpi)
>     print(plot_code)

> choice_df <- read.csv(here("data", "choice_data.csv"))
> choice_df$chose_positive <- ifelse(
>   choice_df$condition == "dislike",
>   as.numeric(choice_df$response != choice_df$correct_answer),
>   as.numeric(choice_df$response == choice_df$correct_answer)
> )
> pos_ID <- choice_df %>%
>   group_by(subID, condition) %>%
>   summarise(prop_positive = mean(chose_positive), .groups = "drop")
> pos_summary <- pos_ID %>%
>   group_by(condition) %>%
>   summarise(mean_pos = mean(prop_positive),
>             se_pos = sd(prop_positive) / sqrt(n()),
>             .groups = "drop")
> pos_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("like", "dislike", "neutral"), function(cd) {
>   x <- pos_ID$prop_positive[pos_ID$condition == cd]
>   alt <- switch(cd, like = "greater", dislike = "less", neutral = "two.sided")
>   tt <- t.test(x, mu = 0.5, alternative = alt)
>   data.frame(condition = cd, mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x),
>              t = as.numeric(tt$statistic), df = as.numeric(tt$parameter),
>              p = tt$p.value, d = (mean(x) - 0.5) / sd(x))
> }))
> pos_tab$p_bonf <- pmin(pos_tab$p * 3, 1)
> pos_tab$sig <- ifelse(pos_tab$p_bonf < 0.001, "***",
>                ifelse(pos_tab$p_bonf < 0.01, "**",
>                ifelse(pos_tab$p_bonf < 0.05, "*", "ns")))

>   choice_data <- choice_data[!is.na(choice_data$RT) &
>                                !(choice_data$RT < 300 | choice_data$RT > 5000), ]
> }
> cat("N participants:", length(unique(choice_data$subID)), "\n")
N participants: 193 
> choice_data$chose_positive <- ifelse(
>   choice_data$condition == "dislike",
>   as.numeric(choice_data$response != choice_data$correct_answer),
>   as.numeric(choice_data$response == choice_data$correct_answer)
> )
> valid_resp <- choice_data$response == choice_data$word1 | choice_data$response == choice_data$word2
> cat("Trials with response not in {word1, word2}:", sum(!valid_resp, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
Trials with response not in {word1, word2}: 0 
> choice_data <- choice_data[valid_resp & !is.na(choice_data$response), ]
> first_choice <- choice_data %>%
>   group_by(subID, condition) %>%
>   slice_min(order_by = trialID, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
>   ungroup() %>%
>   select(subID, condition, trialID, chose_positive)
> cat("Initial-choice rows (subjects x blocks):", nrow(first_choice), "\n")
Initial-choice rows (subjects x blocks): 579 
> CHANCE <- 0.5
> n_conditions <- 3
> results <- first_choice %>%
>   group_by(condition) %>%
>   summarise(
>     n_subjects = n(),
>     n_positive = sum(chose_positive),
>     prop_positive = mean(chose_positive),
>     .groups = "drop"
>   ) %>%
>   rowwise() %>%
>   mutate(
>     bt = list(binom.test(n_positive, n_subjects, p = CHANCE, alternative = "two.sided")),
>     p_binom = bt$p.value,
>     ci_low = bt$conf.int[1],
>     ci_high = bt$conf.int[2]
>   ) %>%
>   ungroup() %>%
>   select(-bt) %>%
>   mutate(
>     p_binom_bonf = pmin(p_binom * n_conditions, 1),
>     sig = ifelse(p_binom_bonf < 0.05, "*", "ns")
>   )
> print(as.data.frame(results))

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In each trial, participants were presented with the sentence “I think you are…” and a positive/negative word pair randomly selected from a list of 64 pairs (e.g., selfish vs. generous).

At the end of each block, participants were asked to rate how much the persona liked them on a scale from 0 (‘Dislike’) to 100 (‘Like’).

Immediately following the behavioral task, participants completed six self-report questionnaires selected a priori to assess their transdiagnostic relationship with social feedback learning, namely the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997).

In the present task, however, there were no reversals and participants completed only 32 trials per condition block.

An attention check was randomly assigned to two of the three blocks, where participants were asked to select a specific word: “Please select to show you are paying attention…”.

Across all three blocks, participants were significantly more likely to choose the positive word than the negative word (Neutral: 73.1%, p < 0.001; Like: 74.6%, p < 0.001; Dislike: 68.9%, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 3), indicating a consistent initial bias towards the positive option across all conditions before any learning had taken place.

The Social Evaluation Learning Task and behavioral results. (a) Participants were instructed to learn about the computer persona’s perspective of themselves, which differs in the probability of positive/negative words being the correct choice.

At the end of each block, participants were asked to provide a single rating on how much the persona disliked them using a Likert scale from 0 (Dislike) to 100 (Like).

Ethics approval statement:

The authors assert that all procedures contributing to this work comply with the ethical standards of the relevant national and institutional committees on human experimentation and with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975, as revised in 2008.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
