How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories.

Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas 'liked,' 'disliked,' or were 'neutral' toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits.

Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed slower decision times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valenced conditions. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms.

These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

Introduction

Learning from social feedback is a vital cognitive process enabling individuals to adjust their behavior based on social cues, such as praise and criticism (Bauer, 1967). This mechanism is crucial for navigating complex social environments, maintaining relationships, and shaping one's self-concept (Boyd et al., 2011; Button et al., 2012; Elder et al., 2022; FeldmanHall & Chang, 2018; Kendal & Watson, 2023; Olsson et al., 2020; Peters et al., 2024; Schröder et al., 2025). In the form of social evaluative feedback, individuals update beliefs about the self and others (Behrens et al., 2008; Diaconescu et al., 2014) from external judgements or feedback which can differ in valence and expectancy (Peters et al., 2024). Social learning can be formally investigated using the framework of reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton & Barto, 2018; Zhang & Gläscher, 2020), a form of error-based learning driven by differences between actual and expected outcomes (i.e., prediction error). Application of the RL framework has revealed distinct biases in social feedback learning in several psychiatric disorders.

Yet, in the context of social feedback learning, existing research has primarily taken a categorical approach often focusing on a single disorder or trait. For example, individuals with social anxiety (Beltzer et al., 2019 (Beltzer et al., , 2023;; Button et al., 2012; Hopkins et al., 2021; Koban et al., 2017 Koban et al., , 2023;; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2019; Zabag et al., 2022 Zabag et al., , 2024) ) and borderline personality disorder (Gregorová et al., 2024; Korn et al., 2016) are biased towards learning more strongly from negative social feedback, whilst depressed individuals conversely do not update their beliefs more strongly following positive compared to negative social feedback (Hobbs et al., 2022; Hoffmann et al., 2024). Narcissistic traits bias perceptions toward evaluators that provide negative feedback about them (Kernis & Sun, 1994; Smalley & Stake, 1996), and individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) demonstrate lowered learning rates and accuracy when learning about others (Cahalan et al., 2026; Schuetze et al., 2017). Additionally, the social dimension of apathy has recently been highlighted (Zhao et al., 2026), yet whether social learning is attenuated amongst apathetic individuals remains underexplored.

Compared to categorical assessments, a transdiagnostic approach to psychopathology (Gillan et al., 2016; Insel et al., 2010; Robbins et al., 2012; Tanaka, 2024) focuses on dimensional traits that cut across multiple disorders. Latent psychological and cognitive constructs or factors of mental health can be extracted that more accurately map onto candidate cognitive processes (Gillan & Seow, 2020). This approach can further be combined with the theorydriven computational modeling of behavior (Zhang, 2023; Sohail & Zhang, 2024), to infer the construct-specific computational processes that characterize a given factor (Wise et al., 2023). Combining transdiagnostic assessments of psychopathology with computational models have identified the specific cognitive processes underlying altered behavior in mental health disorders, including model-based planning (Gillan et al., 2016), metacognition (Rouault et al., 2018), reward processing (Suzuki et al., 2021) and uncertainty (Norbury et al., 2018).

However, a transdiagnostic account of how these traits may differentially influence learning from social feedback is currently not known.

To bridge these research gaps, we used the Social Evaluation Learning Task (SELT) (Button et al., 2012 (Button et al., , 2015)), a well-established paradigm to test participants' learning through valenced social feedback. We adopted a transdiagnostic approach in a non-clinical sample, assessing relevant domains of psychopathology known to affect social behavior, including autism, social anxiety, depression, apathy, narcissism, and BDP. We anticipated transdiagnostic factors reflecting social engagement and mood to be extracted from our questionnaire battery (Gillan et al., 2016; Oka et al., 2025; Schafer & Schiller, 2025). We also hypothesised these factors to differentially moderate social learning effects. Specifically, we expected for social engagement to negatively correlate with a negative learning bias, and for a depressive-mood factor to positively correlate with reduced learning from positive feedback (Button et al., 2012; Hoffmann et al., 2024; Hopkins et al., 2021). This study ultimately provides a nuanced understanding of how overlapping psychiatric traits relate to the ability to learn from social feedback. ticipants (Figure 1a). Each persona followed a unique feedback contingency for the word pair: the positive word was the correct choice 80% of the time for the 'Like' persona, 20% for the 'Dislike' persona, and 50% for the 'Neutral' persona, whereas the negative word was the correct choice 20% of the time for the 'Like' persona, 80% for the 'Dislike' persona, and 50% for the 'Neutral' persona. The feedback contingencies were not communicated to the participants; instead, participants needed to work these out using trial and error. In each trial, participants were presented with the sentence "I think you are…" and a positive/negative word pair randomly selected from a list of 64 pairs (e.g., selfish vs. generous). Participants firstly made a choice between the words, with no enforced time limit, followed by feedback on correctness (500ms) before a fixation cross (400ms). Each block consisted of 32 trials, with the order of the three blocks randomized and counterbalanced across participants. The placement of the two words on the screen was counterbalanced across trials, to avoid motor habituation. At the end of each block, participants were asked to rate how much the persona liked them on a scale from 0 ('Dislike') to 100 ('Like').

Questionnaires

Immediately following the behavioral task, participants completed six self-report questionnaires selected a priori to assess their transdiagnostic relationship with social feedback learning, namely the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997).

Data analysis approach

Behavioral measures

Behavioral data after quality check and cleaning were used to test our hypotheses (4.25% of all trials were excluded; Supplementary Table 1). Three dependent variables were selected as indicators of task behavior: choice accuracy, decision time (DT), and end-of-block persona rating. Choice accuracy was defined as selecting the word whose valence was associated with the feedback contingency; positive words for the 'Like' condition, negative words for the 'Dislike' condition. For the neutral condition, there was no correct response. We coded the 'Like' option as correct response ('Dislike' would reveal same results) to enable joint analysis of all conditions. Raw untransformed DT were used for repeated-measures ANOVA, as subjectlevel mean DTs were normally distributed across all conditions (Shapiro-Wilk tests: W > 0.985; skewness = 0.09-0.24). For trial-level mixed-effects models, we used log-transformed DT values.

Computational modeling framework

The RL framework was applied to quantify the computational processes underlying task behavior. Considering that participants may learn differently from positive versus negative social feedback (Zhang et al., 2020), we tested an RL model (against the simple Rescorla-Wagner model, Rescorla & Wagner, 1972) with two distinct learning rates (𝛼 + and 𝛼 -) for positive and negative prediction errors (PEs) -the difference between the received outcome (O, coded as -1 and 1) and the value (V, initialised at zero) for each trial (t):

As participants preferentially chose the positive option in their initial choice across blocks (see Supplementary Information and Figure S3), we additionally introduced variants of both models with a subject-level scalar parameter representing an initial-value difference to capture this bias.

For all models, a softmax choice function was employed to compute the action probability given action values, where the probability of choosing the positive word over the negative word (coding: positive = 1, negative = 2) was defined as: where the inverse temperature (𝛽 > 0) regulates the stochasticity of how value computation influences choice.

The model space ultimately consisted of four models: single learning rate with no initialvalue bias, dual learning rate with no initial-value bias, single learning rate with initial-value bias, and dual learning rate with initial-value bias. For the initial-value bias models, the softmax 𝛽 was not enforced on the first trial of each block for identifiability reasons. Model estimation was conducted under the hierarchical Bayesian framework (Sohail & Zhang, 2025a) using the {rstan} (Carpenter et al., 2017), and {hBayesDM} (Ahn et al., 2017) R packages.

Four Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains with a minimum of 1000 post-warmup iterations per chain were used. R-hat values for all parameters were below 1.02, indicating excellent model convergence (Gelman & Rubin, 1992). Model comparison was conducted by computing the leave-one-out information criterion (LOOIC) using the {loo} package (Vehtari et al., 2017), which balanced model fit and complexity. Lower LOOIC scores signified superior model performance, and the model with the lowest LOOIC was chosen for further analyses.

Transdiagnostic analyses

An exploratory factor analysis was conducted to identify transdiagnostic factors across the six psychiatric questionnaires used. To account for mixed item types (binary and ordinal), polychoric correlations were computed using the {polycor} package. Factor analysis was performed using the 'fa' function from the {psych} package in R with maximum likelihood estimation and oblique (oblimin) rotation (Costello & Osborne, 2005). Eighty of the eightytwo items (two removed due to zero-variance) across the six questionnaires were included. A Cattell-Nelson-Gorsuch test was used through the {nFactors} package to determine the optimal number of factors. Factor loadings ≥ 0.3 were deemed interpretable. Factor scores were calculated using regression scoring weights and standardized for subsequent analyses.

To uncover transdiagnostic influences on behavioural and computational outcomes, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects regressions with transdiagnostic factor scores, task condition, and their interactions as predictors; a logistic (Bernoulli) model for choice accuracy, and Gaussian models for log-transformed DTs and end-of-block rating. These analyses implemented the three-way model structure: with random intercepts and by-participant random slopes of condition.

Each computational parameter was modelled by task condition and factor scores: with random intercepts for each participant, for the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ), negative learning rate (𝛼 -), their difference (𝛼 + -𝛼 -), and inverse temperature (𝜏 ).

The shared-scalar initial-value bias (initV), being a single value per subject, was modelled at the subject level with no random-effects term:

All Bayesian regression models were fit with the {brms} package v2.23.1 (Bürkner, 2017) in R v4.4.1. We reported the 89% credible interval for posterior inferences (Kreis et al., 2022; 2023; see Supplementary Information for details).

Results

Social feedback valence drives behavioral performance

To test whether feedback valence affected learning accuracy, we examined choice accuracy across the three persona conditions. One-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of condition on choice accuracy (F~(2, 384)~= 208.41, p < .001, 𝜂 2 p = 0.52).

Post-hoc comparisons with Tukey corrections showed that the accuracy was the highest in the 'Like' condition (M = 80.6 ± 14.7%), followed by those from the 'Dislike' (M = 75.9 ± 15.6%) and 'Neutral' (M = 51.6 ± 18.1%) conditions (Figure 1b; Like vs. Neutral: t (192) = 17.259, p < 0.001, Dislike vs. Neutral: t (192) = 14.597, p < 0.001, Like vs Dislike: t (192) = 3.982, p < 0.001).

Next, we examined whether participants learned each persona's evaluation toward themselves at the end of the block. After applying a one-way repeated measures ANOVA on end-of-block ratings revealed a significant effect of condition on ratings (F~(1.85, 354.82)~= 331.93, p < .001, 𝜂 2 p = 0.634; Greenhouse-Geisser corrected, 𝜀 = 0.924, due to a sphericity violation, W = 0.918, p < .001). Post-hoc Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons demonstrated significant differences between all conditions (all p < .001) (Figure 1c).

Finally, we examined whether feedback valence influenced DTs across persona conditions. A one-way repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant effect of condition on DT (F (2,384) = 4.18, p = 0.016), with post-hoc Tukey-corrected comparisons showing participants responded significantly faster in the 'Dislike' (M =1604 ± 476ms) condition compared to 'Neutral' (M = 1698 ± 529ms) (p = 0.009), while other pairwise comparisons were not significant ('Like' condition: M = 1667 ± 466ms, Figure 1d).

Distinct learning rates for positive and negative feedback underlie social evaluative learning

To determine whether participants exhibited asymmetric learning from positive versus negative feedback, we compared the four computational models crossing the learning-rate structure with the initial-value bias. Model comparison revealed that the dual-learning-rate model with the shared initial-value bias provided the best overall fit, outperforming the next-best model (ΔLOOIC = 18.4; Supplementary Table 2), confirming that participants processed positive and negative social feedback differently. Parameters from the winning model showed goodto-excellent recovery, and posterior predictive checks broadly captured the key patterns in our behavioral data (see Supplementary Figures 1 and 2).

Next, we tested whether learning rates varied as a function of feedback valence and persona condition. A learning-rate valence (positive vs negative) by condition (Like, Dislike, Neutral) repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) revealed a significant main effect of learning-rate valence (F (1,192) = 465.51, p < 0.001) and condition (F~(1.27, 243.94)~= 52.27, p < 0.001), and a significant interaction (F~(1.27, 243.82)~= 111.26, p < 0.001), indicating that the relationship between feedback valence and learning varied across conditions (Figure 2a). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons using Tukey's adjustment showed the positive learning rate was significantly higher in both the 'Like' and 'Dislike' conditions than in 'Neutral' (both p < 0.001), but did not differ between 'Like' and 'Dislike' (t (192) = 1.83, p = 0.162). For negative learning rates, the 'Like' condition showed significantly lower learning rates than both 'Neutral' (t (192) = 5.40, p < 0.001) and 'Dislike' (t (192) = 5.26, p < 0.001), which did not significantly differ from each other (t (192) = 1.82, p = 0.166).

We similarly examined whether choice stochasticity, indexed by the inverse temperature (𝜏 ), varied across conditions. A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) revealed a significant effect of condition on 𝜏 (F~(1.25, 240.82)~= 115.50, p < 0.001, 𝜂 2 p = 0.11) (Figure 2a). Tukey-corrected post-hoc comparisons showed that 𝜏 was significantly higher in both the 'Like' (M = 2.14) and 'Dislike' (M = 2.20) conditions than in 'Neutral' (M = 1.62; Like vs Neutral: t (192) = 25.90, p < 0.001; Dislike vs Neutral: t (192) = 11.93, p < 0.001), indicating more deterministic choice under valenced feedback, but did not differ between 'Like' and 'Dislike' (t (192) = 1.10, p = 0.513).

To examine whether individual differences in learning rates predicted behavioral performance, we ran Kendall's rank (𝜏 ) correlations between computational parameters and choice accuracy across conditions. Both the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ; Kendall's 𝜏 = 0.262, p < 0.001) and the difference between the positive and negative learning rates -the positive learning bias -(𝛼 + -𝛼 -; Kendall's 𝜏 = 0.195, p < 0.001) were positively associated with accuracy in the 'Like' condition after Bonferroni correction (Figure 2b-c). However, no significant relationship was observed for the negative learning rate (𝜏 = -0.055, p = 0.264).

As a follow-up analysis, we computed the mean trial-averaged learned value of the positiveword from the winning model (V positive ) and correlated it with participants' end-of-block ratings, to bridge computational learning signals with acquired social evaluations. Kendall's 𝜏 correlations between mean V positive and ratings were significant in the Neutral (𝜏 = 0.161, z = 3.29, p = .001, r = 0.251) and Like (𝜏 = 0.235, z = 4.78, p < .001, r = 0.360) conditions, but not in the Dislike condition (𝜏 = 0.064, z = 1.30, p = .194, r = 0.10) (Figure 2d). All these results highlight a direct link between the capacity to learn from social feedback and its recognition in social contexts reflected in task performance.

Transdiagnostic factors are differentially associated with learning parameters and task behavior

Our EFA analysis revealed that a 3-factor solution best accounted for the questionnaire data (25.8% of variances explained), identifying transdiagnostic dimensions of psychopathology that may relate to social feedback learning. Based on the strongest individual item loadings (Figure 3), factors were labelled accordingly as 'Social Avoidance', with higher scores reflecting reduced social motivation and increased avoidance, 'Emotional Insensitivity', where higher scores indicate high apathy and difficulties evaluating and empathizing with others, and 'Depressive Self-Identity', where higher scores correspond to low mood, low self-esteem and negative self-identity.

To examine whether transdiagnostic factors predicted computational mechanisms underlying social feedback learning, we fit Bayesian mixed-effects models with computational parameters from the winning model as dependent variables (Figure 4a-c). Condition effects on learning parameters were robust, with the Like condition credibly increasing positive learning rates (posterior mean = 0.075, 89% CrI [0.070, 0.081]) and decreasing negative learning rates (mean = -0.036, 89% CrI [-0.047, -0.026]), while the Dislike condition credibly increased both positive learning rates (mean = 0.067, 89% CrI [0.062, 0.073]) and positive learning bias (mean = 0.060, 89% CrI [0.048, 0.073]). Additionally, the 'Social Avoidance' factor credibly predicted negative learning rates (mean = 0.023, 89% CrI [0.007, 0.040]) and learning rate difference (mean = -0.022, 89% CrI [-0.040, -0.005]) in opposite directions. Specifically, individuals with higher scores on this 'Social Avoidance' factor learned more from negative social feedback, reflecting a negative learning bias. No two-way interactions between condition and transdiagnostic factors were credible, nor did any other transdiagnostic factors show a credible association with computational learning parameters (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero), suggesting that the negative learning bias observed is specific to traits related to social avoidance and low social motivation.

We next sought to understand whether the three transdiagnostic factors moderated the effect of feedback valence on behavioral performance. To do so, we fit a series of three-way mixedeffects regression models with transdiagnostic factors, learning rate parameters (𝛼 + and 𝛼 -), and valence conditions as predictors for task performance. This revealed credible main effects towards choice accuracy (Figure 5a) for both 'Like' (posterior mean = 1.407, 89% CrI [1.227, 1.584]) and 'Dislike' conditions (mean = 1.097, 89% CrI [0.927, 1.270]), consistent with our repeated measures ANOVA analysis. We also observed a credible positive main effect of the positive learning rate (𝛼 + ; mean = 1.688, 89% CrI [0.021, 3.315]), alongside credible two-way interactions between the 'Like' (mean = -0.333, 89% CrI [-0.513, -0.152]) and 'Dislike' (mean = -0.222, 89% CrI [-0.390, -0.050]) conditions and 'Emotional Insensitivity', indicating that higher scores on this factor attenuated the benefits in accuracy typically observed in value-congruent learning contexts. In addition, the negative learning rate (𝛼 -) showed credible positive interactions with both the 'Dislike' condition (mean = 1.138, 89% CrI [0.181, 2.102]) and 'Social Avoidance' (mean = 0.832, 89% CrI [0.094, 1.587]), such that faster learning from negative feedback was associated with higher accuracy in the Dislike condition and among individuals higher in Social Avoidance. No three-way interactions were credible (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero).

Finally, we investigated whether transdiagnostic factors and learning rate parameters similarly influenced decision time (Figure 5b). The 'Dislike' condition showed a credible main effect (posterior mean = -0.086, 89% CrI [-0.156, -0.016]) indicating faster decisions overall. The negative learning rate parameter also showed a credible main effect (mean = 0.543, 89% CrI [0.246, 0.844]), two-way interaction with 'Social Avoidance' (mean = -0.359, 89% CrI [-0.702, -0.021]) and three-way interaction with the 'Like' condition and Social Avoidance (mean = 0.478, 89% CrI [0.148, 0.810]), suggesting that individuals with higher Social Avoidance scores and higher negative learning rates exhibited slower decision times specifically in the 'Like' condition.

Discussion

The current study investigated how behavioral traits affect individuals' learning from social feedback utilizing a transdiagnostic approach and reinforcement learning. Model comparison revealed that a simple reinforcement learning model with an initial value difference and separate learning rates for positive and negative feedback best quantifies the data, indicating asymmetric learning processes. Learning rates were found to vary by task condition, with the positive learning rate higher in both valenced ('Like' and 'Dislike') conditions than in the 'Neutral' condition. Individual differences in positive learning rates and positive learning bias were also both associated with higher choice accuracy in the 'Like' condition. This suggests that individuals who learn more strongly from positive feedback make more accurate evaluative judgements in socially positive contexts.

Our factor analysis extracted three robust transdiagnostic dimensions: 'Social Avoidance', 'Emotional Insensitivity' and 'Depressive Self-Identity'. These dimensions partly overlap with previous studies extracting transdiagnostic factors of psychopathology from general population samples (Gillan et al., 2016; Hoven et al., 2023; Oka et al., 2025). A previous study also previously labeled a 'Social Avoidance' factor strongly loaded items from measures of social anxiety, autism and apathy (Schafer & Schiller, 2025), and items for Depression and Borderline personality were found to load onto the same factor alternatively labelled 'Mood' (Schafer & Schiller, 2025). On-the-other-hand, the presence of an 'Emotional Insensitivity' factor not reported previously reflects the current study's specific focus towards assessing social evaluative learning. Indeed, this factor loaded items from the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) and Apathy Motivation Index (AMI), questionnaires not included together in previous studies.

The extraction of this factor highlights the ability to understand and interpret the emotions of others as an important transdiagnostic dimension of social learning.

We further found significant associations between extracted transdiagnostic dimensions and task-related assessments of social evaluation learning. Specifically, we show that a latent Social Avoidance dimension, cutting across social anxiety and related traits, is selectively associated with a negative learning bias and slower decision times towards positive social feedback. This finding extends previous research using categorical assessments of social anxiety and BPD demonstrating similar learning biases using reinforcement learning models (Hoffmann et al., 2024; Koban et al., 2017 Koban et al., , 2023;; Korn et al., 2016) and increased deliberation in response to positive social information (Hunter et al., 2022; Van Der Molen et al., 2014).

The Social Avoidance factor further loaded items from the 'Social Motivation' subscale of the Apathy Motivation Index (AMI). Though existing research on apathy has mainly focused on motivation control and effort-based decision-making (Costello et al., 2024; Derosiere et al., 2025), recent accounts have identified the motivation to socially engage as a key transdiagnostic measure given its comorbid presentation across multiple disorders (Barkus & Badcock, 2019) that may have distinct clinical and neurobiological correlates and respond differently to treatments (Chetcuti et al., 2026).

A second transdiagnostic factor, Emotional Insensitivity, reflecting lowered empathy and problems inferring the emotions of others, attenuated performance in both Like and Dislike conditions. As empathy requires accurate emotional identification (Bird & Viding, 2014; Shamay-Tsoory & Hertz, 2022), individuals with reduced empathy are less capable of discerning changes in other's emotions (Coll et al., 2017; Gonzalez-Gadea et al., 2014). This is commonly observed among individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) who show difficulties in social interactions (Bolis & Schilbach, 2017) due to challenges with understanding the intentions of others (Rosenthal et al., 2019). In the current study, measures from the Autism Quotient (AQ-10) and 'Emotional Sensitivity' subscale of the Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) loaded strongly onto the Emotional Insensitivity factor, both of which may be obscured in categorical assessments or questionnaires. Emotional apathy is robustly associated with prosocial behavior across different contexts (Contreras-Huerta et al., 2022), with higher levels predicting a lowered tendency to help others (Lockwood et al., 2017). Yet, few studies have specifically investigated its role with social reward learning. In a study of dementia patients, those with high emotional apathy were found to demonstrate impaired learning towards social rewards (Wong et al., 2023). Our results further show that difficulties with interpreting the emotions of others directly impairs the ability to accurately evaluate social feedback.

The present study has some potential limitations. Although we compared four RL models assessing selective learning from positive and negative feedback, along with an initialvalue bias, this represents a relatively restricted model space. We deliberately adopted a parsimonious model specification without additional parameters (e.g., choice lapse, perseveration), because such parameters may only be informative in longer tasks or reversal-learning paradigms (e.g., Sugawara & Katahira, 2021), where lapses and choice-history effects are more readily dissociated from learning and decision noise. In the present task, however, there were no reversals and participants completed only 32 trials per condition block. Given this limited number of observations, adding further parameters would risk weak identifiability and parameter trade-offs. We also opted for not including an outcome sensitivity parameter, as outcomes in our task were binary rather than varying in their magnitude. We therefore prioritized a simpler model that captured the core learning and choice processes supported by the task design and available data, though our winning model may nonetheless be regarded as best-fitting only among these candidate models.

Additionally, our sample is mainly comprised of females and consisted exclusively of university students. This may explain the lack of any significant results with the Depressive Self-Identity factor, which strongly loaded items assessing depressive symptoms centred on guilt, lack of satisfaction and suicidal ideation. The reported Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores in our sample (M = 12.52 ± 9.34) primarily reflect minimal (0-13) or mild (14-19) depression (Beck et al., 1996). However, depressive symptomatology may only emerge with more severe cases than those present in our non-clinical student population (Insel et al., 2010). Furthermore, given the non-clinical nature of the sample which consisted primarily of female university students, our findings should be interpreted as reflecting subclinical trait dimensions. Further studies within clinical and more diverse samples are warranted before drawing conclusions about clinical mechanisms. Future studies should therefore aim to capture a wider range of depressive symptoms across a more diverse sample (Geng et al., 2022), including recent approaches that take the advantage of large language models by simulating individuals with various personal profiles (Sohail & Zhang, 2025b; Li et al., 2026), both in laboratory and naturalistic conditions (Wang et al., 2026).

Taken together, combining a transdiagnostic measure of behavior with computational modelling, our study identifies key behavioral signatures of biased social evaluation learning.

Computational modelling revealed that participants exhibited asymmetric learning from positive versus negative social feedback, with learning rates varying by feedback valence. A transdiagnostic factor reflecting social anxiety and motivational deficits biased social learning towards negatively salient information. An 'Emotional Insensitivity' factor capturing difficulties in empathy and mentalizing was associated with sensitivity to positive social feedback.

These findings demonstrate how transdiagnostic traits influence social evaluative learning, identifying candidate computational processes that can be targeted in future studies.

Data quality measures and checks

An attention check was randomly assigned to two of the three blocks, where participants were asked to select a specific word: "Please select <word> to show you are paying attention...". Participants who failed either of the two attention checks were removed from the analysis. Trials with a decision time greater than 5000ms or less than 300ms were also excluded, accounting for 4.25% of trials. Trial exclusion rates were not significantly different across conditions ( 2 (2) = 5.87, p = 0.053), and was not significantly associated with any transdiagnostic factor score (all 𝜏 0.081, all p ≥ .115; Supplementary Table 1).

To test whether participants accurately learned the reward contingencies, we determined whether accuracy across valenced conditions exceeded chance level (50%). Indeed, one-sample t-tests confirmed that accuracy exceeded chance (50%) in valenced conditions (Like: t (192) = 28.94, p < 0.001; Dislike: t (192) = 23.02, p < 0.001) but not Neutral (t (192) = 1.24, p = 0.215).

Questionnaire battery and factor loadings

Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10) (Allison et al., 2012), a 10-item screening instrument for autistic traits, where higher scores indicate greater social communication difficulties and rigidity. Items are rated as "Agree" or "Disagree," and scored dichotomously (0 or 1), yielding a total score range of 0-10.

Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) (Connor et al., 2000), a 17-item measure of social anxiety symptoms. Participants rate how much each statement (e.g., fear of embarrassment) applies to them, with higher scores indicating greater social anxiety. Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = "Not at all" to4 = "Extremely"), producing a total score range of 0-68.

Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) (Beck et al., 1996), a 21-item inventory assessing depressive symptoms such as sadness, pessimism, and anhedonia. Higher scores reflect more severe depressive tendencies, and each item is rated from 0 to 3, leading to a total score range of 0-63.

Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) (Ang et al., 2017), an 18-item scale measuring apathy across behavioral and social domains. We used the total score as an index of general apathy (higher scores = greater apathy/lower motivation). Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = "Strongly disagree" to4 = "Strongly agree"), giving a total score range of 0-72.

Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ) (Back et al., 2013), a short 6-item version of a narcissism scale, with higher scores indicating stronger narcissistic tendencies.

Items are rated on a 6-point scale (1 = "Disagree strongly" to6 = "Agree strongly"), so total scores range from 6 to 36.

Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) checklist (First et al., 1997), a 10-item yes/no screening checklist for BPD features, where higher scores indicate greater severity. One item with no variance in our sample was removed, so scores were based on the remaining 9 items, with a total score range of 0-9.

For the Social Avoidance factor, the highest average loadings came from the SPIN questionnaire (M = 0.57, ± 0.11), with significant contributions from AMI (M = 0.19 ± 0.23) and AQ-10 (M = 0.16 ± 0.14). The 'Emotional Insensitivity' factor showed only moderate loadings from AMI (M = 0.20 ± 0.26) and AQ (M = 0.17 ± 0.22), with no other questionnaires contributing meaningfully. Finally, Depressive Self-Identity was dominated by items from the BDI questionnaire (M = 0.59 ± 0.10), followed by BPD (M = 0.36 ± 0.09), with no other questionnaires reaching the 0.15 average loading threshold.

Model comparison and winning model specification

The model space constituted four models: M1a (single learning rate, no initial-value bias), M1b (dual learning rate, no initial-value bias), M2a (single learning rate, with initial-value bias), and M2b (dual learning rate, with initial-value bias). (b) Next, we simulated 193 synthetic participants whose parameters were sampled using the hierarchical structure implemented in the Stan model.

Individual-level parameters 𝜙 𝑖 were generated using non-centered parameterization in probit-transformed space, then transformed to natural parameter bounds via effect coding and the cumulative normal distribution function, preserving the model's hierarchical structure and parameter constraints. We repeated this procedure for all individual-level parameters of the winning model. (c) Then, we used the winning model as a generative tool to simulate behavioral data for our social evaluation learning task, namely, to simulate choices for 96 trials per participant (32 trials per condition). Individuals' choices (denoted as D𝑖 ) were sampled from the sampling distribution conditional on individual-level parameters (𝜙 i ) from the previous step (i.e., likelihood function): 𝐷 𝑖 ∼ 𝑝(𝐷 𝑖 | 𝜙 𝑖 ) (9) (d) We fit the model to the simulated data ( D𝑖 ) in the same way as we did for the real data obtaining parameter estimates (i.e., posterior distributions) at both the group-level (e.g., μ 𝜑 , σ 𝜑 ) and the individual level (e.g., φ 𝑖 ). (e) Finally, we compared whether the posterior distributions recovered the true datagenerating parameters. At the group level, we assessed whether the true parameter values fell within the 95% highest density interval (HDI) of the recovered posterior distributions for each iteration, and report coverage rates (percentage of iterations where true value falls within 95% HDI) across the 20 iterations (Supplementary Figure 1A).

At the individual level, we computed Spearman's rank correlations (𝜌) between the true and recovered parameters for each parameter and condition combination within each iteration, then aggregated these correlations across iterations using Fisher's Z transformation to obtain mean correlation coefficients (Supplementary Figure 1B).

The parameter recovery analyses initially revealed differential recoverability across individuallevel parameters, with the positive learning rate showing lower correlations compared to negative learning rates. Examining the fitted parameters revealed relatively low betweensubject variability for the positive learning rate (CV = 0.06-0.17), whereas in contrast, the negative learning rate showed high variability (CV = 0.65-0.90) (Supplementary Table 3).

To test whether low variability of this parameter caused the observed differences with recovery, we re-ran parameter recovery after artificially increased the group-level standard deviation of 𝛼 + while keeping all other parameters at empirical values (Supplementary Figure 1). Increasing this variability subsequently improved recovery across all three conditions for 𝛼 + (Neutral: 𝜌 = 0.239 to 0.508; Like: 𝜌 = 0.363 to 0.601; Dislike: 𝜌 = 0.274 to 0.541). In contrast, 𝛼 - recovery remained good and stable (𝜌 = 0.59-0.68).

Posterior predictive checks

To validate that the winning model could generate behavioral patterns consistent with the observed data, we conducted posterior predictive checks using a generative simulation approach. We selected 4,000 posterior samples from the winning model's MCMC chains, where for each sample, we extracted the individual-level parameters (𝛼 + , 𝛼 -, 𝜏 ) for all 193 participants across all three conditions and used the model to simulate a complete synthetic dataset of 96 trials per participant (32 trials per condition), maintaining the same task structure and feedback contingencies as in the original experiment. We then analysed each simulated dataset using the same statistical procedures applied to the observed data. Specifically, we cal- To test whether this also reflected low 𝛼 + variance, we fit the model to simulated data with inflated 𝛼 + variance as described above, and re-generated 4,000 posterior predictive datasets.

Doing so fully recovered the observed Like accuracy (observed = 68.7%, predicted = 70.4%, 95% HDI: 68.1%, 72.7%, Bayesian p-value = 0.133). The remaining conditions were also well-recovered: Neutral (observed = 53.4%, predicted = 52.7%, 95% HDI: 50.5%, 55.0%, p = 0.585) and Dislike (observed = 68.5%, predicted = 68.5%, 95% HDI: 66.2%, 70.8%, p = 0.986), with all observed values falling within their respective 95% prediction intervals.

Initial choice within conditions

To check whether there was an initial bias in choice across conditions, we examined the first choice trial of each block (before any feedback had been received), and tested the proportion of participants choosing the positive word against chance (50%) with an exact binomial test, Bonferroni-corrected across the three blocks. Across all three blocks, participants were significantly more likely to choose the positive word than the negative word (Neutral: 73.1%, p < 0.001; Like: 74.6%, p < 0.001; Dislike: 68.9%, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 3), indicating a consistent initial bias towards the positive option across all conditions before any learning had taken place.

Supplementary

Significant predictors of participants' ratings

Separate to our primary series of analyses, we also ran a Bayesian mixed-effects model predicting participants' end-of-block ratings to determine whether feedback valence was reflected in participants' impression of how much the fictional persona liked them. This model (Supplementary Figure 4) revealed credible main effects of task condition for both 'Like' (mean = 28.81, 89% CrI [24.74, 32.90]) and 'Dislike' (mean = -17.34, 89% CrI [-21.61, -13.02]) personas, consistent with our manipulation of social feedback valence. No credible main effects of transdiagnostic factors or learning rate parameters were observed, and no two-way or threeway interactions between factors, learning rate parameters, and conditions were credible (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero; Supplementary Table 4).
