Parameter recovery

After model fitting, we confirmed the identifiability of parameters through parameter recovery.

We repeated the following procedure for 20 iterations. Denoting 𝜙 as a generic parameter, we iterated the following steps:

Subjective ratings and learned value

To verify that participants' explicit social appraisals tracked the feedback contingencies across conditions, we examined whether model-derived learned values predicted self-reported ratings of how much the feedback agent liked them. This served as a manipulation check, confirming that the computational learning signals captured by the model corresponded to participants' subjective experience of the social feedback.

For each participant and condition, we reconstructed the trial-by-trial trajectory of V positivethe learned value of the positive-word option -by replaying the Rescorla-Wagner update rule forward using each participant's posterior mean 𝛼 + and 𝛼 -estimates. Specifically, V positive was initialised to zero at the start of each block and updated on each valid trial according to: where 𝛼 + was applied following positive outcomes and 𝛼 -following negative outcomes.

The mean V positive across all valid trials within each block was taken as the learned social value for that condition. This quantity reflects the degree to which participants learned that the agent responded positively to their choices: values approaching +1 indicate strong learned association between positive choices and positive feedback, while negative values indicate the inverse.

Explicit ratings were collected via a continuous slider (0-100) at the end of each block, with participants indicating how much they felt the feedback agent liked them. We computed Kendall's 𝜏 correlations between mean V positive and ratings separately for each condition.

Transdiagnostic regression models

To determine the relationship between observed behaviour, model parameters and transdiagnostic factors, we ran a series of Bayesian multilevel regressions fit using the {brms} package v2.23.1 (Bürkner, 2017), using the {rstan} v2.32.7 backend (Carpenter et al., 2017). Priors were weakly informative and set per outcome family. All eight models were sampled with 4

Markov chains of 4,000 iterations each (2,000 warmup, 2,000 post-warmup per chain; 8,000 post-warmup draws total). Convergence was excellent throughout (R̂m ax = 1.0074, ESS min = 1,076 out of 8,000 draws), with zero divergent transitions and zero transitions exceeding the maximum treedepth.

Choice stochasticity and initial valuation

Complementing our primary set of regression models predicting learning rate parameters from the winning model, we also tested whether the inverse temperature parameter (𝜏 , choice stochasticity) varied by condition and transdiagnostic factor score. Doing so revealed credible main effects of both the 'Like' (posterior mean = 0.53, 89% CrI [0.46, 0.59]) and 'Dislike' conditions (mean = 0.58, 89% CrI [0.51, 0.65]), indicating more deterministic choice behavior in both valenced conditions relative to Neutral (Supplementary Table 5). No transdiagnostic factor showed a credible main effect or condition interaction with 𝜏 (all 89% credible intervals spanned zero). We separately tested whether transdiagnostic factor scores predicted the initial positivity bias parameter introduced by the winning model. No transdiagnostic factor showed a credible association (Depressive Self-Identity: mean = 0.001, 89% CrI [-0.003, 0.004]; Social Avoidance: mean = -0.002, 89% CrI [-0.006, 0.001]; Emotional Insensitivity: mean = -0.002, 89% CrI [-0.005, 0.001]; Supplementary Table 6), indicating no relationship between baseline positivity bias and the extracted transdiagnostic dimensions.

culated mean choice accuracy for each condition and conducted repeated-measures ANOVA with post-hoc pairwise comparisons (Tukey-corrected). To evaluate model fit, we calculated Bayesian p-values as the proportion of predicted statistics more extreme than the corresponding observed statistic (two-tailed), with p-values < 0.05 indicating circumstances where the model fails to capture the observed data pattern. Posterior predictive checks (PPCs) on the empirical data showed that the winning model captured the ordering of accuracy across conditions, with observed values falling within the 95% prediction intervals for the Neutral (observed = 49.8%, predicted = 50.0%, 95% HDI: 48.7%, 51.2%, Bayesian p = 0.636) and Dislike (observed = 76.2%, predicted = 74.3%, 95% HDI: 71.9%, 76.6%, Bayesian p = 0.058) conditions. The model continued to underestimate accuracy in the Like condition (observed = 80.9%, predicted = 78.3%, 95% HDI: 76.1%, 80.4%, Bayesian p = 0.005). The predicted overall condition effect remained weaker than observed (observed F = 361.43, predicted mean F = 253.28, Bayesian p = 0.011), and predicted pairwise differences were smaller than observed for Neutral vs. Like (p = 0.021) and Neutral vs. Dislike (p = 0.125), while the Like vs. Dislike difference was well captured (p = 0.636).

The winning model (M2b) implemented a hierarchical Rescorla-Wagner framework with asymmetric learning rates for reward (𝛼 + ) and punishment (𝛼 -), alongside an inverse temperature parameter (𝜏 ) governing choice stochasticity, and a subject-level shared-scalar baseline initialvalue bias applied at the first trial of each block. Parameters were estimated using Bayesian hierarchical modeling with non-centered parameterization and effect coding for within-subject condition contrasts.

(a) We randomly drew one joint sample of group-level parameters from the joint posterior group-level distribution of the winning model, a Rescorla-Wagner model with separate learning rates for positive and negative outcomes. That is, a group-level mean (𝜇 𝜙 ) and a group-level standard deviation (𝜎 𝜙 ) of the parameter 𝜙. We repeated this procedure for all group-level parameters of the winning model: Supplementary Figure 1. Parameter recovery for the winning computational model (a) At the group level, true group-level means fell within the recovered posterior distributions across parameters and conditions. (b) At the individual level, parameter recovery was good across all learning-related parameters once between-subject variance was inflated. Supplementary Figure 2. Posterior predictive checks of the winning model fit to simulated data with inflated 𝛼 + variance, assessed through choice accuracy. Predicted versus observed mean choice accuracy per condition (block). Coloured points show predicted means across posterior predictive datasets, the orange point reflects the observed mean of the simulated data.

Supplementary Figure 4.

Coefficients from the Bayesian three-way model for participants' ratings. Posterior mean coefficients for ratings showed only condition main effects for Like and Dislike. Yellow = credible positive effects (89% credible interval excludes zero), Blue = credible negative effects (89% credible interval excludes zero), grey = noncredible effects (89% credible interval includes zero). Error bars = 89% credible intervals.
